paper.title: ExploreNet : Learning Where to Explore in Diffusion GRPO
paper.abstract:
Abstract Group-relative RL methods such as Flow-GRPO post-train image generators by exploring with isotropic Gaussian noise added at every denoising step.
This noise decides which rollouts the model learns from, yet it perturbs every channel and spatial position of the latent equally.
In this paper, we instead show that latent elements differ in how much they change the generated image, so exploration should adapt to these differences.
We introduce ExploreNet to learn an adaptive exploration distribution. ExploreNet is a policy that predicts a noise scale for every latent element from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt, before any reward is observed; it is trained on the reward spread of each rollout group and discarded after training, leaving inference unchanged.
On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ExploreNet improves held-out GenEval2 by 14 % 14\% over Flow-GRPO, transfers to two independent compositional benchmarks and five preference and image-quality models, and reaches a 67.2 % 67.2\% human preference win-rate.
Overall, across our group-relative diffusion RL experiments, we find that exploration is learnable, the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude, and rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning unleashes the potential of image generators for alignment ( Black et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , from instruction following ( Li et al., 2026b ) and human preference ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , to personalization ( Dang et al., 2025 ) and reasoning ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . GRPO is a common online RL algorithm that samples a group of rollouts for each prompt and learns from the differences in their rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Flow-GRPO enables GRPO in flow-matching models by adding isotropic Gaussian noise at every otherwise deterministic denoising step ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2025 ) . This noise alone decides the rollouts and thereby provides the exploration that guides the reinforcement learning. One line of work targets the noise, showing that the isotropic noise injection of Flow-GRPO results in excessive or insufficient stochasticity, and proposing to adjust noise levels by denoising steps ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . Within each step, however, the same noise scale still applies to every channel and spatial position of the latent. Our key insight is that the latent is unevenly sensitive . Perturbing some latent channels restructures the scene, while perturbing others changes only details (Section 4.5 ). Exploration should therefore adapt to how sensitive each latent element is , yet isotropic noise allocates it equally over fine details and scene structure. Another line of work directly manipulates rollout groups for a better learning signal by oversampling rollouts, observing their rewards, and training on an informative subset ( Ge et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . However, post-hoc rollout selection relies on knowing the reward before choosing which rollouts to train on, and each update pays for rollouts it discards. Instead, we frame learning the exploration distribution as a reinforcement learning problem . The noise drawn at each denoising step is an action, and its reward arrives when the image is scored after the last denoising step. More specifically, we propose ExploreNet , a diffusion post-training method that learns an adaptive noise scale for each latent element, sets it before each denoising step without observing any reward, and keeps every rollout it samples for training. ExploreNet is a separate transformer network that predicts noise scales from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt (Figure 1 ), and is trained jointly with the denoiser on the reward spread of each prompt group. It is removed after training, so the trained denoiser keeps its sampler and inference cost. Figure 1: Deterministic flow-matching sampling adds no randomness beyond the initial noise, which limits exploration and leaves the policy ratio without a tractable transition density. Flow-GRPO samples rollouts with isotropic Gaussian perturbations and updates the denoiser f θ f_{\theta} with group-relative advantages A p , i A_{p,i} . ExploreNet g ϕ g_{\phi} predicts the scale map s ϕ s_{\phi} before each denoising step. The denoiser keeps ℒ θ \mathcal{L}_{\theta} , and ExploreNet optimizes ℒ ϕ \mathcal{L}_{\phi} with the normalized reward spread B p B_{p} . Inference uses only the trained denoiser. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al., 2024 , SD3.5-M) trained with GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) , ExploreNet outperforms Flow-GRPO across a broad image-generation evaluation suite. Learning the exploration distribution improves held-out GenEval2 by 14 % 14\% , and the gain transfers to two independent compositional benchmarks and five preference and image-quality models. Human raters prefer ExploreNet to Flow-GRPO and the pretrained checkpoint 67.2 % 67.2\% of the time. Further ablations show that the gain comes from the shape of the exploration distribution. Noise raised uniformly to ExploreNet ’s average variance performs worse than Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet ’s scales are largest in the latent channels whose perturbation changes the image most. Rollout quality is also more effective than rollout quantity. With 8 rollouts per prompt, ExploreNet exceeds Flow-GRPO with 24, and with half as many rollouts, it matches privileged post-hoc selection, which observes every reward. Our contributions are as follows: • ExploreNet , which learns a noise scale for every latent element at each denoising step, set from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt before any reward is observed, at unchanged inference cost. • Experiments on SD3.5-M showing that exploration is learnable, with gains over Flow-GRPO across a broad image-generation evaluation suite and in human preference. • Controlled comparisons showing that the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude and that rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity.

ExploreNet is a second policy whose action is the noise: before the reward is known, it predicts a scale for each latent element from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt, and it is trained afterward from the reward spread of each rollout group. sections.heading: 3.2 Training from Reward Spread
sections.text: Figure 2: With all else fixed, selecting high-spread groups yields the fastest learning. A noise action has no reward of its own: the reward arrives only for the finished image, and the denoiser learns from the reward differences among rollouts of the same prompt. A noise choice can therefore be credited only through the group it helps produce, and what a group offers the denoiser is its reward spread. A group whose rewards are equal gives every rollout zero advantage, and Flow-GRPO divides each group’s advantages by its reward spread σ R , p \sigma_{R,p} (Eq. 2 ), so a group whose rewards are nearly equal yields advantages that amplify small, uninformative differences. To measure the effect of spread directly, we generate 16 rollouts per prompt and train on 8 selected to have the smallest reward spread, selected at random, or selected to have the greatest reward spread, with the rollout pool, update group size, and optimizer fixed. Greatest-spread selection learns fastest and smallest-spread selection slowest (Figure 2 ), and the ordering holds on eight of nine evaluation metrics (Appendix A.3 ). sections.heading: 3.3 Joint Training and Inference
sections.text: Each training iteration samples P P prompts and G G rollouts per prompt using the current denoiser and ExploreNet , and the same rewards train both policies at two granularities. The rollout advantage A p , i A_{p,i} measures each rollout’s reward relative to its prompt group and weights the policy gradient of the denoiser, and the group advantage B p B_{p} measures each group’s reward spread relative to the other groups in the iteration and weights the policy gradient of ExploreNet . The two networks minimize ℒ θ \mathcal{L}_{\theta} and ℒ ϕ \mathcal{L}_{\phi} with separate optimizers. At inference, we discard g ϕ g_{\phi} and sample the trained denoiser with the standard flow-matching sampler.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We test our central hypothesis: allocating rollout noise across latent elements improves group-relative diffusion RL. Our experiments address three questions: (1) Does ExploreNet improve the trained denoiser? (2) Why does it work? (3) Where does it place the noise? Training. All training experiments fine-tune SD3.5-M ( Esser et al., 2024 ) on the GenEval2 training split ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) with the Flow-GRPO denoising objective ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Within each comparison, methods use the same training prompts, reward implementation, denoising schedule, rollout group size, optimizer settings for the denoiser, training duration, and checkpoint cadence. Appendix A.1 gives the complete training hyperparameters and computational cost. Baselines and controls. We compare ExploreNet with Flow-GRPO and two controls: • Flow-GRPO uses the isotropic noise of Eq. 1 with the default noise level λ = 0.7 \lambda=0.7 and 24 rollouts per prompt group, the same group size as ExploreNet . • Matched isotropic control replaces ExploreNet ’s learned scale map with a single constant, 1.41 1.41 , for every latent element, which matches the average variance of ExploreNet ’s noise (Appendix A.4 ). It removes only the allocation to test whether the gain comes from the shape or the magnitude of ExploreNet ’s exploration. • Privileged post-hoc selection generates 48 rollouts per prompt, observes every reward, and trains on the 24 with the greatest reward spread. It uses twice the rollouts and reward evaluations of ExploreNet , so it tests whether learned allocation, set before any reward is observed, can match or exceed selection after sampling. Automatic evaluation. On the held-out GenEval2 prompts, we score the trained models with the GenEval2 metric and with a VLM judge based on GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) . To evaluate transfer performance, we use GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , VVRBench-Fast ( Li et al., 2026b ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , Aesthetic ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) , and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . Appendix B.1 specifies the prompt sets, metric implementations, generation settings, and other evaluation details. Human evaluation. Three annotators each make 216 pairwise preference judgments (A, B, or Tie) over 72 unique prompts from pairs drawn from SD3.5-M, Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet . Win-rate is calculated as each model’s total score divided by the number of comparisons it appears in (win receives a score of 1 1 , tie receives a score of 0.5 0.5 ). The prompts are sampled equally from DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) , PartiPrompts ( Yu et al., 2022 ) , DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , T2I-CompBench ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , the OCR prompt set from Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , and VVRBench ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Appendix B.2 gives the annotation protocol details.

sections.heading: 4.3 Decomposing Magnitude and Shape of Exploration
sections.text: ExploreNet explores more than Flow-GRPO, with about twice its average noise variance, which follows from the shape of its scale maps (Section 3 ), and shapes its exploration by allocating noise unevenly across latent elements. We ask whether the gain comes from the magnitude or the shape of this exploration. To separate the two, we compare ExploreNet with two alternatives from Section 4.1 that increase exploration without shaping it: the matched isotropic control raises its magnitude, and privileged post-hoc selection raises the number of rollouts. Magnitude without shape lowers performance. The matched isotropic control adds noise with the same average variance as ExploreNet but spreads it uniformly across latent elements. On the same training seed, raising the noise uniformly lowers GenEval2 below Flow-GRPO ( 0.437 0.437 versus 0.498 0.498 ), while allocating the same variance raises it to 0.567 0.567 (Table 2 ). ExploreNet also exceeds the control on eight of nine metrics. Two alternative parameterizations let ExploreNet shift the overall level of its noise, one clipping g ϕ g_{\phi} ’s output without standardization and one applying a learned scale and bias after standardization, and both end training below ExploreNet (Appendix A.2 ). sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Reward-based post-training of diffusion and flow models. Diffusion and flow models have been post-trained with reward-weighted likelihood ( Lee et al., 2023 ) , policy gradients ( Black et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , differentiable rewards ( Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) , preference optimization ( Wallace et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2024b ) , and KL- or entropy-regularized stochastic control ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) . GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) was adapted to flow models by Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO, which convert the deterministic sampler into a stochastic one ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2025 ) , and later methods learn the reward adversarially or optimize group preferences directly ( Mao et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Follow-up work changes which denoising steps explore, through sliding stochastic windows, branching, or high-entropy steps ( Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , how much each step explores, as DenseGRPO does by calibrating a single noise level per step in a separate pass over sampled trajectories ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or how rewards are credited to steps ( He et al., 2025 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Savani et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . ExploreNet instead learns the shape of the exploration distribution across latent elements from the current state; its scale map multiplies the per-step noise coefficient a t a_{t} , so a per-step schedule sets the level of the noise at each step and ExploreNet sets its allocation within the step. Constructing informative rollouts. Post-hoc selection methods observe the rewards of additional rollouts, with ProGRPO keeping subsets of high reward spread and Smart-GRPO searching over candidate noise ( Ge et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . DiffExp perturbs classifier-free guidance and prompt-phrase weights, and E 2 PO optimizes prompt embeddings for semantic spread ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Initial-noise methods optimize the starting latent of a sample or learn prompt-conditioned initial-noise distributions ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Miao et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2025 ) . These approaches spend additional rollouts and reward evaluations, perturb the conditioning, or act before denoising begins. ExploreNet sets the noise at every denoising step, before any reward is observed, and is trained jointly with the denoiser. Learned noise and exploration. Diffusion models have learned reverse variances and covariances ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) , data-dependent forward processes ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , and spatially adaptive or reweighted noise ( Lavda et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and inference-time samplers add flow-orthogonal perturbations or learn noise schedules ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Lim and Gandelsman, 2026 ) ; these methods shape noise to model the data or to improve samples. In flow-model RL, Coefficients-Preserving Sampling, related analyses, and Precise study how much stochasticity the sampler should inject, with the noise fixed by design ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) , and diversity-preserving objectives regularize what the model is trained toward ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Sorokin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . In deep RL, parameter noise and state-dependent exploration replace fixed action noise with structured perturbations ( Plappert et al., 2018 ; Fortunato et al., 2018 ; Raffin et al., 2022 ) . ExploreNet brings state-dependent exploration to diffusion RL, learning the exploration distribution from the reward spread of each rollout group and discarding it at inference.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Group-relative diffusion RL learns only from the alternatives its sampler produces, yet the exploration distribution that produces them follows a fixed schedule that treats every latent element alike. Latent elements differ in how much they change the generated image, and ExploreNet makes the exploration distribution trainable so that it can adapt to these differences. It predicts a noise scale for every latent element from the current state of generation, learns from the reward spread of each rollout group jointly with the denoiser, and is discarded after training, so the final model is sampled exactly as before. Across our experiments, exploration proves learnable, the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude, and rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity. Exploration is therefore a design axis of diffusion RL in its own right, alongside reward design and per-step noise schedules.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The exploration distribution q ϕ q_{\phi} is a diagonal Gaussian; correlated noise across latent elements, such as low-rank or spatially structured covariances, could explore coherent changes such as moving an object as a whole. ExploreNet learns only the transition noise, and the same framework could learn other sources of rollout variation, such as the guidance scale or the initial noise, jointly with it. ExploreNet learns from the reward spread of each rollout group. Other group statistics, such as the spread of individual reward components or of verifier constraint families, could train separate exploration distributions for different objectives. Video latents add a temporal axis, and ExploreNet can allocate exploration across frames as well as channels and spatial positions. Group-relative RL for autoregressive and discrete-diffusion generators explores by sampling tokens at a fixed temperature, and a learned per-position temperature could play the role of ExploreNet ’s scale map. ExploreNet is a second SD3.5-M transformer; a lightweight head on the denoiser could predict the same scale maps from its own features. Channel sensitivity is a property of the SD3.5-M latent space, so a trained ExploreNet could be reused across rewards and fine-tuning runs of the same base model. The scale maps identify which latent channels control the content of a generated image, which could guide diverse sampling, localized editing, and the perturbations of best-of- N N and other inference-time search methods. A theoretical account of when the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude, relating latent sensitivity to the reward spread of rollout groups, remains open.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: ExploreNet improves reward-based fine-tuning of text-to-image models and inherits the risks of the models it fine-tunes, including the generation of misleading or harmful images. The human evaluation asked annotators to compare generated images and to rate visual changes; the annotators were graduate students who volunteered, and Appendix B.2 describes the protocol.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: Section 3 and Appendix A.1 specify the objectives, architecture, and all training hyperparameters. Appendix B.1 specifies the prompt sets, metric implementations, generation settings, and aggregation. All code is released.

sections.heading: A.1 Hyperparameters and Compute
sections.text: The image experiments use SD3.5-M at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution with 25 sampling and evaluation denoising steps, classifier free guidance 4.5 4.5 , Flow-GRPO noise level λ = 0.7 \lambda=0.7 , and 24 rollouts per prompt in the main setting. Training uses 64 H100 GPUs over eight nodes. Each rank samples microbatches of 3, with 8 sampling batches per epoch, one inner epoch, and gradient accumulation 4. In the main setting, each training iteration therefore samples P = 64 P=64 prompts with G = 24 G=24 rollouts each (1,536 images), and both policies take two optimizer updates on these rollouts. The update counts reported throughout the paper are optimizer updates. The group-size-8 runs keep this schedule and 1,536 images per iteration, so each iteration samples P = 192 P=192 prompts with G = 8 G=8 rollouts each. Both the denoiser and ExploreNet use rank 32 LoRA adapters with LoRA scale 64 on the SD3.5-M attention projections. The denoising optimizer uses Adam with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and gradient norm clipping at 1.0. ExploreNet initializes a separate SD3.5-M transformer from the pretrained model, freezes its base weights, and trains its rank 32 LoRA parameters in fp32. Its Adam optimizer uses learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} and zero weight decay. The final parameterization normalizes the output per sample and clips log standard deviation directly to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , with a standard-deviation floor of 10 − 6 10^{-6} during normalization. Reward normalization uses an additive constant of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Both clipped objectives use clip range ϵ = 10 − 4 \epsilon=10^{-4} and advantages clipped to [ − 5 , 5 ] [-5,5] . The exploration objective applies a KL penalty of weight β ϕ = 10 − 3 \beta_{\phi}=10^{-3} toward the unit Gaussian, and the denoising objective applies a KL penalty of weight β θ = 0.04 \beta_{\theta}=0.04 toward the pretrained denoiser, for both Flow-GRPO and ExploreNet . The denoising and exploration policy optimizers are stepped after the same backward pass. The 48-to-24 privileged post-hoc selection baseline doubles rollout generation and GenEval2 reward calls relative to the 24 rollout runs, then keeps the 12 lowest- and 12 highest-reward samples, the subset of 24 with the greatest reward spread. Measured over steps 2160 through 2580, Flow-GRPO requires 151.7 151.7 seconds per optimizer update and ExploreNet requires 189.4 189.4 seconds. ExploreNet therefore takes 1.25 × 1.25\times as long per update, corresponding to 161.8 161.8 versus 202.0 202.0 GPU hours per 60 updates, including periodic evaluation and checkpointing. During training, ExploreNet holds a second 2.5-billion-parameter SD3.5-M transformer in memory, and both methods fit a per-rank microbatch of 3 on 80 GB H100 GPUs. At inference, both methods use 25 denoiser evaluations and ExploreNet is not used. sections.heading: Benchmarks and prompt sets.
sections.text: GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) contains 720 training prompts and a fixed 80-prompt held-out split covering object presence, count, attributes, and spatial relations. Each prompt is decomposed into atomic visual questions. Qwen3-VL-2B assigns probability to the accepted short answers, and the image score is the geometric mean across questions. GenEval2 is the sole reward used to train the main models. On the same 80-prompt test set, VLM Judge scores prompt alignment from 1 to 5. Official GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) uses 553 prompts with four generations per prompt, giving 2,212 evaluated images. VVRBench-Fast ( Li et al., 2026b ) contains 820 prompts sampled from VVRBench Core across its attainable complexity levels. Its frozen, model-free verifier evaluates grounding, cardinality, spatial, size, and topology constraints from executable scene specifications. We report dense VVR, the mean dense verifier score over all 820 prompts. We evaluate PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) on 500 unique prompts from the Pick-a-Pic v1 validation split. We evaluate HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) on its complete 3,200-prompt benchmark, comprising 800 prompts each for anime, concept art, paintings, and photo. We report the mean PickScore, the four HPS domain means, and their unweighted macro average. We evaluate HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , Aesthetic score, and ImageReward on the full 200-prompt DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) set and fixed 1,000-prompt lists from PartiPrompts ( Yu et al., 2022 ) , DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and T2I-CompBench ( Huang et al., 2023 ) . The aesthetic score uses the LAION improved aesthetic predictor ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) , with a CLIP ViT-L/14 image encoder and its released linear MSE head; ImageReward uses ImageReward-v1.0 ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . We average each metric within a prompt list and report the unweighted mean of the four list means.

sections.heading: Generation and aggregation.
sections.text: Checkpoints are saved and evaluated every 60 optimizer updates. For the main comparison, we evaluate the checkpoint at step 3000 without selecting by evaluation score. Evaluation uses the trained denoiser with the deterministic flow-matching sampler without ExploreNet . The primary comparison comprises three independent training seeds per method and three GenEval2 evaluation passes per seed. All other automatic benchmarks use one pass per training seed. Each model generates one image per prompt except for official GenEval, which uses four. Matched methods receive the same prompts and initial latent seeds. We average evaluation passes within each training seed, then report the mean and sample standard deviation across seeds. Controlled and robustness experiments use one training seed unless their corresponding result states otherwise. Flow-GRPO and ExploreNet runs are paired by training seed (42, 123, and 456, labeled 1 to 3); Table 7 reports every seed.

sections.heading: B.2 Human Evaluation
sections.text: The preference and displacement studies use the same 72 matched triplets of pretrained, Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet outputs described in Section 4 . Each of the six prompt suites contributes 12 examples, and each training seed contributes four examples within a suite. For DrawBench, PartiPrompts, DPG-Bench, T2I-CompBench, and the Flow-GRPO OCR prompt set ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , we draw 12 distinct prompts uniformly without replacement using a fixed study seed. For VVRBench, we draw one prompt from each of 12 prespecified strata spanning composition tier and difficulty. We then shuffle each suite with the same fixed seed and assign prompts cyclically across the three training seeds. The panel is fixed before image generation, and the three models use the same generation seed for each prompt. The preference interface presents the prompt and two unlabeled candidates. It instructs annotators to prioritize satisfaction of the full prompt and then visual quality, reserving a tie for cases in which neither image is meaningfully preferable. Trial order and candidate position are independently randomized. Three annotators evaluate all 216 pairwise comparisons, giving 648 judgments. Preference rates count each tie as one half for each model. Confidence intervals resample prompts while retaining all ratings associated with each sampled prompt. Pairwise exact agreement among the three annotators ranges from 56.9 % 56.9\% to 72.7 % 72.7\% , and 47.7 % 47.7\% of comparisons receive unanimous labels. sections.heading: Change from pretrained outputs.
sections.text: The displacement study uses the same 72 matched triplets and three complete annotators. The interface presents the pretrained output as a labeled reference between blinded Flow-GRPO and ExploreNet candidates. Annotators identify which candidate differs more from the reference in scene content or composition. The instructions define this criterion through entities, attributes, counts, spatial arrangement, viewpoint, and framing, while excluding differences limited to color, lighting, texture, rendering style, or image quality. Trial order and candidate position are independently randomized for each annotator. Across 216 ratings, ExploreNet is selected 181 times, Flow-GRPO 25 times, and 10 judgments are ties. The tie-adjusted ExploreNet rate is 86.1 % 86.1\% , with a 95% CI of [ 80.1 , 91.4 ] [80.1,91.4] . ExploreNet receives a majority on 62 of 72 prompts, Flow-GRPO on 6, and 4 prompts have no majority. Pairwise exact agreement ranges from 77.8 % 77.8\% to 80.6 % 80.6\% , with unanimous labels on 70.8 % 70.8\% of prompts.

sections.heading: Human perceptual evaluation.
sections.text: The human study uses prompts at fixed manifest indices 0, 20, 26, 47, 67, and 98 from the GenEval2 training set and the pretrained, Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet denoisers. For every model and prompt, we generate a deterministic reference and intervene on each of the 16 latent channels with both signs. This gives 288 trials, each containing a reference and two perturbed images, and 576 perturbed images in total. Model, channel, and perturbation sign are hidden from annotators. Nine annotators participated, and each trial contributes exactly three independent ratings. When four ratings were available, we dropped one at random for each trial using a fixed seed before aggregation. Each image receives an ordinal change magnitude rating from 0 for no obvious visible difference to 4 for a very large difference. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.38329v1 [cs.CV] 29 Sep 2026 ExploreNet : Learning Where to Explore in Diffusion GRPO Shuyue Stella Li Xiaochuang Han Yulia Tsvetkov Luke Zettlemoyer Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: stelli@cs.washington.edu Affiliation: https://github.com/stellalisy/ExploreNet Abstract Group-relative RL methods such as Flow-GRPO post-train image generators by exploring with isotropic Gaussian noise added at every denoising step. This noise decides which rollouts the model learns from, yet it perturbs every channel and spatial position of the latent equally. In this paper, we instead show that latent elements differ in how much they change the generated image, so exploration should adapt to these differences. We introduce ExploreNet to learn an adaptive exploration distribution. ExploreNet is a policy that predicts a noise scale for every latent element from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt, before any reward is observed; it is trained on the reward spread of each rollout group and discarded after training, leaving inference unchanged. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ExploreNet improves held-out GenEval2 by 14 % 14\% over Flow-GRPO, transfers to two independent compositional benchmarks and five preference and image-quality models, and reaches a 67.2 % 67.2\% human preference win-rate. Overall, across our group-relative diffusion RL experiments, we find that exploration is learnable, the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude, and rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning unleashes the potential of image generators for alignment ( Black et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , from instruction following ( Li et al., 2026b ) and human preference ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , to personalization ( Dang et al., 2025 ) and reasoning ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . GRPO is a common online RL algorithm that samples a group of rollouts for each prompt and learns from the differences in their rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Flow-GRPO enables GRPO in flow-matching models by adding isotropic Gaussian noise at every otherwise deterministic denoising step ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2025 ) . This noise alone decides the rollouts and thereby provides the exploration that guides the reinforcement learning. One line of work targets the noise, showing that the isotropic noise injection of Flow-GRPO results in excessive or insufficient stochasticity, and proposing to adjust noise levels by denoising steps ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . Within each step, however, the same noise scale still applies to every channel and spatial position of the latent. Our key insight is that the latent is unevenly sensitive . Perturbing some latent channels restructures the scene, while perturbing others changes only details (Section 4.5 ). Exploration should therefore adapt to how sensitive each latent element is , yet isotropic noise allocates it equally over fine details and scene structure. Another line of work directly manipulates rollout groups for a better learning signal by oversampling rollouts, observing their rewards, and training on an informative subset ( Ge et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . However, post-hoc rollout selection relies on knowing the reward before choosing which rollouts to train on, and each update pays for rollouts it discards. Instead, we frame learning the exploration distribution as a reinforcement learning problem . The noise drawn at each denoising step is an action, and its reward arrives when the image is scored after the last denoising step. More specifically, we propose ExploreNet , a diffusion post-training method that learns an adaptive noise scale for each latent element, sets it before each denoising step without observing any reward, and keeps every rollout it samples for training. ExploreNet is a separate transformer network that predicts noise scales from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt (Figure 1 ), and is trained jointly with the denoiser on the reward spread of each prompt group. It is removed after training, so the trained denoiser keeps its sampler and inference cost. Figure 1: Deterministic flow-matching sampling adds no randomness beyond the initial noise, which limits exploration and leaves the policy ratio without a tractable transition density. Flow-GRPO samples rollouts with isotropic Gaussian perturbations and updates the denoiser f θ f_{\theta} with group-relative advantages A p , i A_{p,i} . ExploreNet g ϕ g_{\phi} predicts the scale map s ϕ s_{\phi} before each denoising step. The denoiser keeps ℒ θ \mathcal{L}_{\theta} , and ExploreNet optimizes ℒ ϕ \mathcal{L}_{\phi} with the normalized reward spread B p B_{p} . Inference uses only the trained denoiser. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al., 2024 , SD3.5-M) trained with GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) , ExploreNet outperforms Flow-GRPO across a broad image-generation evaluation suite. Learning the exploration distribution improves held-out GenEval2 by 14 % 14\% , and the gain transfers to two independent compositional benchmarks and five preference and image-quality models. Human raters prefer ExploreNet to Flow-GRPO and the pretrained checkpoint 67.2 % 67.2\% of the time. Further ablations show that the gain comes from the shape of the exploration distribution. Noise raised uniformly to ExploreNet ’s average variance performs worse than Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet ’s scales are largest in the latent channels whose perturbation changes the image most. Rollout quality is also more effective than rollout quantity. With 8 rollouts per prompt, ExploreNet exceeds Flow-GRPO with 24, and with half as many rollouts, it matches privileged post-hoc selection, which observes every reward. Our contributions are as follows: • ExploreNet , which learns a noise scale for every latent element at each denoising step, set from the current latent, the denoising step, and the prompt before any reward is observed, at unchanged inference cost. • Experiments on SD3.5-M showing that exploration is learnable, with gains over Flow-GRPO across a broad image-generation evaluation suite and in human preference. • Controlled comparisons showing that the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude and that rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity. 2 Preliminaries: Group-Relative RL for Flow Models Following DDPO and Flow-GRPO, we treat denoising as a Markov decision process ( Black et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Our experiments address three questions: (1) Does ExploreNet improve the trained denoiser? (2) Why does it work? (3) Where does it place the noise? Training. All training experiments fine-tune SD3.5-M ( Esser et al., 2024 ) on the GenEval2 training split ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) with the Flow-GRPO denoising objective ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Within each comparison, methods use the same training prompts, reward implementation, denoising schedule, rollout group size, optimizer settings for the denoiser, training duration, and checkpoint cadence. Appendix A.1 gives the complete training hyperparameters and computational cost. Baselines and controls. We compare ExploreNet with Flow-GRPO and two controls: • Flow-GRPO uses the isotropic noise of Eq. 1 with the default noise level λ = 0.7 \lambda=0.7 and 24 rollouts per prompt group, the same group size as ExploreNet . • Matched isotropic control replaces ExploreNet ’s learned scale map with a single constant, 1.41 1.41 , for every latent element, which matches the average variance of ExploreNet ’s noise (Appendix A.4 ). It removes only the allocation to test whether the gain comes from the shape or the magnitude of ExploreNet ’s exploration. • Privileged post-hoc selection generates 48 rollouts per prompt, observes every reward, and trains on the 24 with the greatest reward spread. It uses twice the rollouts and reward evaluations of ExploreNet , so it tests whether learned allocation, set before any reward is observed, can match or exceed selection after sampling. Automatic evaluation. On the held-out GenEval2 prompts, we score the trained models with the GenEval2 metric and with a VLM judge based on GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) . To evaluate transfer performance, we use GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , VVRBench-Fast ( Li et al., 2026b ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , Aesthetic ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) , and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . Appendix B.1 specifies the prompt sets, metric implementations, generation settings, and other evaluation details. Human evaluation. Three annotators each make 216 pairwise preference judgments (A, B, or Tie) over 72 unique prompts from pairs drawn from SD3.5-M, Flow-GRPO, and ExploreNet . Win-rate is calculated as each model’s total score divided by the number of comparisons it appears in (win receives a score of 1 1 , tie receives a score of 0.5 0.5 ). The prompts are sampled equally from DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) , PartiPrompts ( Yu et al., 2022 ) , DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , T2I-CompBench ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , the OCR prompt set from Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , and VVRBench ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Appendix B.2 gives the annotation protocol details. 4.2 ExploreNet Improves the Trained Denoiser We begin by comparing ExploreNet with Flow-GRPO, with the unmodified SD3.5-M as a pretrained reference. Across three matched training seeds, ExploreNet outperforms Flow-GRPO on every metric in the evaluation suite (Table 3 ). The GenEval2 gain persists across the final five checkpoints and under a paired bootstrap over evaluation prompts (Appendix C.2 ). Diffusion and flow models have been post-trained with reward-weighted likelihood ( Lee et al., 2023 ) , policy gradients ( Black et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , differentiable rewards ( Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) , preference optimization ( Wallace et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2024b ) , and KL- or entropy-regularized stochastic control ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) . GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) was adapted to flow models by Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO, which convert the deterministic sampler into a stochastic one ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2025 ) , and later methods learn the reward adversarially or optimize group preferences directly ( Mao et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Follow-up work changes which denoising steps explore, through sliding stochastic windows, branching, or high-entropy steps ( Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , how much each step explores, as DenseGRPO does by calibrating a single noise level per step in a separate pass over sampled trajectories ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or how rewards are credited to steps ( He et al., 2025 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Savani et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . ExploreNet instead learns the shape of the exploration distribution across latent elements from the current state; its scale map multiplies the per-step noise coefficient a t a_{t} , so a per-step schedule sets the level of the noise at each step and ExploreNet sets its allocation within the step. Constructing informative rollouts. Post-hoc selection methods observe the rewards of additional rollouts, with ProGRPO keeping subsets of high reward spread and Smart-GRPO searching over candidate noise ( Ge et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . DiffExp perturbs classifier-free guidance and prompt-phrase weights, and E 2 PO optimizes prompt embeddings for semantic spread ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Initial-noise methods optimize the starting latent of a sample or learn prompt-conditioned initial-noise distributions ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Miao et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2025 ) . These approaches spend additional rollouts and reward evaluations, perturb the conditioning, or act before denoising begins. ExploreNet sets the noise at every denoising step, before any reward is observed, and is trained jointly with the denoiser. Learned noise and exploration. Diffusion models have learned reverse variances and covariances ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) , data-dependent forward processes ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , and spatially adaptive or reweighted noise ( Lavda et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and inference-time samplers add flow-orthogonal perturbations or learn noise schedules ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Lim and Gandelsman, 2026 ) ; these methods shape noise to model the data or to improve samples. In flow-model RL, Coefficients-Preserving Sampling, related analyses, and Precise study how much stochasticity the sampler should inject, with the noise fixed by design ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) , and diversity-preserving objectives regularize what the model is trained toward ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Sorokin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . In deep RL, parameter noise and state-dependent exploration replace fixed action noise with structured perturbations ( Plappert et al., 2018 ; Fortunato et al., 2018 ; Raffin et al., 2022 ) . ExploreNet brings state-dependent exploration to diffusion RL, learning the exploration distribution from the reward spread of each rollout group and discarding it at inference. 6 Conclusion Group-relative diffusion RL learns only from the alternatives its sampler produces, yet the exploration distribution that produces them follows a fixed schedule that treats every latent element alike. Latent elements differ in how much they change the generated image, and ExploreNet makes the exploration distribution trainable so that it can adapt to these differences. It predicts a noise scale for every latent element from the current state of generation, learns from the reward spread of each rollout group jointly with the denoiser, and is discarded after training, so the final model is sampled exactly as before. Across our experiments, exploration proves learnable, the shape of the exploration distribution outweighs its magnitude, and rollout quality is more effective than rollout quantity. Exploration is therefore a design axis of diffusion RL in its own right, alongside reward design and per-step noise schedules. Limitations The exploration distribution q ϕ q_{\phi} is a diagonal Gaussian; correlated noise across latent elements, such as low-rank or spatially structured covariances, could explore coherent changes such as moving an object as a whole. ExploreNet learns only the transition noise, and the same framework could learn other sources of rollout variation, such as the guidance scale or the initial noise, jointly with it. ExploreNet learns from the reward spread of each rollout group. Other group statistics, such as the spread of individual reward components or of verifier constraint families, could train separate exploration distributions for different objectives. Video latents add a temporal axis, and ExploreNet can allocate exploration across frames as well as channels and spatial positions. Group-relative RL for autoregressive and discrete-diffusion generators explores by sampling tokens at a fixed temperature, and a learned per-position temperature could play the role of ExploreNet ’s scale map. ExploreNet is a second SD3.5-M transformer; a lightweight head on the denoiser could predict the same scale maps from its own features. Channel sensitivity is a property of the SD3.5-M latent space, so a trained ExploreNet could be reused across rewards and fine-tuning runs of the same base model. The scale maps identify which latent channels control the content of a generated image, which could guide diverse sampling, localized editing, and the perturbations of best-of- N N and other inference-time search methods.
